lesson.title: Splitting a Difference Before You Integrate
lesson.summary: The difference rule mirrors the sum rule, letting you integrate term by term when functions are subtracted: ∫[f(x) - g(x)]dx = ∫f(x)dx - ∫g(x)dx.
lesson.body:
The sum rule let you break apart an integrand built from addition. The exact same idea applies when an integrand involves subtraction. The difference rule states: ∫[f(x) - g(x)]dx = ∫f(x)dx - ∫g(x)dx. Just as with the sum rule, this works because differentiation itself splits cleanly across subtraction: d/dx[F(x) - G(x)] = F'(x) - G'(x), so reversing the process preserves that same structure.

Together, the sum rule and the difference rule mean that any polynomial integrand, no matter how many terms it has or which signs connect them, can be integrated one term at a time. This is what makes integrating expressions like 6x^2 - 4x + 3 manageable: you do not need a new rule for every combination of pluses and minuses, only the power rule, the constant rule, and the ability to split the expression apart term by term.

Let's work through a combined example that uses a difference, a sum, and a constant all at once: ∫(6x^2 - 4x + 3)dx. Split it into three separate integrals: ∫6x^2 dx - ∫4x dx + ∫3 dx. Integrate each piece. First, ∫6x^2 dx = 6 · (x^3/3) = 2x^3. Second, ∫4x dx = 4 · (x^2/2) = 2x^2. Third, using the constant rule, ∫3 dx = 3x. Assembling these with the correct signs from the original expression gives 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + C.

Check the full result by differentiating term by term: d/dx[2x^3] = 6x^2, d/dx[-2x^2] = -4x, d/dx[3x] = 3, and d/dx[C] = 0. Adding these derivatives back together gives 6x^2 - 4x + 3, which matches the original integrand exactly. This example is a good one to keep in mind going forward, since it shows how the power rule, the constant rule, the sum rule, and the difference rule all work together on a single polynomial, each rule handling one term while the constant of integration is added only once, at the very end.
